I joined @GoogleDeepMind to develop a research program on the economics of AGI. Today, together with Andrew Koh ( @andrewjkoh ) and Shane Legg ( @ShaneLegg ), we are incredibly excited to release The Economics of Intelligence, the first in a series of projects from our group on how AGI will change the economy. How do capability improvements transform the economy, and when? In this project, we define thresholds of economic capabilities, e.g., minimal AGI, based on how they transform the economy. We then track how the economy–market structure, employment, and wages–changes during the transition across capability regimes. We have seen exponential increases in what AI agents can do but the broader economy seems almost remarkably unchanged. Part of the reason is that the solo AI agent is the wrong economic object; economic transformation is an equilibrium outcome where organizations compete. Looking at how intelligence functions within organizations, transformation will depend on when two key capability thresholds are crossed: competence (gains on individual skills, e.g., coding, math) and coordination (gains on ability of agents to cooperate and work together). We show that what economic transformation looks like depends on whether AI becomes supercompetent, supercooperative, or both—the regime of artificial superintelligence (ASI). Tracking this transition shows why the real visible transformation may come from improvements in coordination—a capability most benchmarks don’t yet track. Past a certain threshold, AI capabilities can break the Coasian ceiling on firm size and lead to an economy that looks drastically different than the one we see today. Two main takeaways: 1. To understand the path of transformation, we should be tracking agentic coordination more closely. 2. The impact of AI will likely show up in wages before market structure or employment. We are really excited about this paper. Excited to hear people’s thoughts. Link: institute.deepmind.com/essay… Video

I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus. The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future. I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf. Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent. Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade. Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine. Why now We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten. But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible. This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition. More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest. I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building. Believing before consensus My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine. I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today. I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?” Then we work backward together to make it happen. In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI , before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue. In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models. In 2025, Anna and Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point. The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale. @linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike. @tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues. @Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies. Making the ambition possible Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight. These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work. This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger. Thank you To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together. Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. To Roelof, for bringing me into Sequoia and believing in me from the beginning. Alfred and Roelof, you have been mentors in investing and in life. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me. To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap. Let’s get to work!

Workers in six occupations do 79 tasks the government's official occupational taxonomy has yet to add. That work is worth about $140B a year in wages. That taxonomy is called O*NET, the U.S. Department of Labor's database of the tasks each occupation involves. Workers use it to help with job transitions, and economists use it to estimate which jobs AI will change. If the lists are incomplete, so are the estimates. Today we're releasing TaskNet, an open-source task catalog built on O*NET and updated for how AI is changing work. Built with researchers from Stanford, the O*NET Resource Center, and NBER. processed.summary: Cette journée met en lumière les progrès rapides de l'IA, avec le lancement de modèles très puissants comme Gemini 4 Carbon et les aperçus de Genie 4, qui repoussent les frontières de ce que l'IA peut faire. On observe aussi l'émergence de nouvelles façons d'interagir avec les ordinateurs, notamment par la voix, et des réflexions profondes sur l'impact économique de l'IA générale (AGI) sur l'emploi et les salaires. Enfin, plusieurs outils innovants et ressources d'apprentissage sont partagés, illustrant la diversité des applications et l'accessibilité croissante de cette technologie.

glossaire.definition: Une IA hypothétique capable d'apprendre et de réaliser n'importe quelle tâche intellectuelle humaine, pas seulement des tâches spécifiques.
Un système d'IA parmi les plus avancés et performants qui existent, repoussant les limites de ce qui est possible.
L'utilisation d'un modèle d'IA entraîné pour faire des prédictions ou générer des réponses sur de nouvelles données.
De petits fragments de texte (mots ou parties de mots) que les modèles d'IA traitent et mesurent pour évaluer la quantité d'information.
Une Interface de Programmation d'Application, un ensemble de règles permettant à différents logiciels de communiquer et d'utiliser les fonctionnalités d'un autre programme.
Une branche de l'IA utilisant des réseaux de neurones très complexes, inspirés du cerveau, pour apprendre à partir de grandes quantités de données.
Une approche de l'IA qui manipule des symboles et des règles logiques, plutôt que des statistiques sur de grandes masses de données.

category_summaries.actu: L'actualité est riche en annonces de nouveaux modèles d'IA performants, comme Gemini 4 Carbon qui excelle dans de multiples tests et le futur Genie 4. Les entreprises du secteur, telles qu'Alphabet, annoncent des croissances impressionnantes tirées par leurs investissements en IA et le déploiement de fonctionnalités innovantes, comme les modes vocaux. On assiste également à des avancées dans la vérification de preuves mathématiques complexes par ordinateur et la publication de nouvelles ressources pour analyser l'impact de l'IA sur l'emploi.
category_summaries.tips: Pour les débutants passionnés, une ressource inestimable est mise gratuitement à disposition : le livre 'Deep Learning with Python'. category_summaries.idees: Les discussions du jour portent sur des questions fondamentales : les limites actuelles de l'intelligence de l'IA face à la puissance de calcul disponible, les implications économiques de l'Intelligence Artificielle Générale (AGI), notamment sur l'emploi et la coordination des agents IA. Des réflexions sont aussi partagées sur la manière d'investir dans l'IA et sur la critique des discours alarmistes concernant l'avenir de cette technologie.
category_summaries.outils: De nouveaux outils basés sur l'IA sont présentés, offrant des expériences interactives comme la 'démontage' virtuel d'objets en 3D avec Perplexity Computer ou la création de designs personnalisés grâce à Vyb. Des mises à jour facilitent également l'utilisation de modèles d'IA localement, permettant aux utilisateurs d'expérimenter plus facilement.

Aujourd'hui, avec Andrew Koh (@andrewjkoh) et Shane Legg (@ShaneLegg), nous sommes incroyablement enthousiastes à l'idée de publier "L'Économie de l'Intelligence", le premier d'une série de projets de notre groupe sur la façon dont l'AGI va transformer l'économie. Comment les améliorations de capacités transforment-elles l'économie, et quand ? Dans ce projet, nous définissons des seuils de capacités économiques, par exemple, une AGI minimale, en fonction de la manière dont elles transforment l'économie. Nous suivons ensuite l'évolution de l'économie – structure du marché, emploi et salaires – pendant la transition entre différents régimes de capacités. Nous avons constaté des augmentations exponentielles de ce que les agents IA peuvent faire, mais l'économie en général semble remarquablement inchangée. Une partie de la raison est que l'agent IA seul est le mauvais objet économique ; la transformation économique est un résultat d'équilibre où les organisations sont en concurrence. En examinant comment l'intelligence fonctionne au sein des organisations, la transformation dépendra du franchissement de deux seuils de capacités clés : la compétence (gains sur les compétences individuelles, par exemple, le codage, les mathématiques) et la coordination (gains sur la capacité des agents à coopérer et à travailler ensemble). Nous montrons que l'aspect de la transformation économique dépendra de la question de savoir si l'IA devient super-compétente, super-coopérative ou les deux – le régime de la superintelligence artificielle (ASI). Le suivi de cette transition montre pourquoi la vraie transformation visible pourrait venir des améliorations de la coordination – une capacité que la plupart des benchmarks ne suivent pas encore. Au-delà d'un certain seuil, les capacités de l'IA peuvent briser le "plafond de Coase" sur la taille des entreprises et conduire à une économie radicalement différente de celle que nous connaissons aujourd'hui. Deux points clés à retenir : 1. Pour comprendre le chemin de la transformation, nous devrions suivre la coordination "agentique" plus attentivement. 2. L'impact de l'IA se manifestera probablement d'abord sur les salaires avant la structure du marché ou l'emploi. Nous sommes vraiment enthousiastes à propos de ce document. Impatients d'entendre vos réflexions. Lien : institute.deepmind.com/essay… Vidéo
idees.text_original: I joined @GoogleDeepMind to develop a research program on the economics of AGI. Today, together with Andrew Koh ( @andrewjkoh ) and Shane Legg ( @ShaneLegg ), we are incredibly excited to release The Economics of Intelligence, the first in a series of projects from our group on how AGI will change the economy. How do capability improvements transform the economy, and when? In this project, we define thresholds of economic capabilities, e.g., minimal AGI, based on how they transform the economy. We then track how the economy–market structure, employment, and wages–changes during the transition across capability regimes. We have seen exponential increases in what AI agents can do but the broader economy seems almost remarkably unchanged. Part of the reason is that the solo AI agent is the wrong economic object; economic transformation is an equilibrium outcome where organizations compete. Looking at how intelligence functions within organizations, transformation will depend on when two key capability thresholds are crossed: competence (gains on individual skills, e.g., coding, math) and coordination (gains on ability of agents to cooperate and work together). We show that what economic transformation looks like depends on whether AI becomes supercompetent, supercooperative, or both—the regime of artificial superintelligence (ASI). Tracking this transition shows why the real visible transformation may come from improvements in coordination—a capability most benchmarks don’t yet track. Past a certain threshold, AI capabilities can break the Coasian ceiling on firm size and lead to an economy that looks drastically different than the one we see today. Two main takeaways: 1. To understand the path of transformation, we should be tracking agentic coordination more closely. 2. The impact of AI will likely show up in wages before market structure or employment. We are really excited about this paper. Excited to hear people’s thoughts. Link: institute.deepmind.com/essay… Video

Les commanditaires du fonds comprendront Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (mon professeur de Stanford et conseiller scientifique en chef de TSMC), et d'autres dont le travail a façonné notre industrie et ma façon de penser l'avenir de l'IA. Je resterai associé chez Sequoia et continuerai à siéger aux conseils d'administration pour le compte de Sequoia. Sequoia a été ma maison pendant les 11 dernières années. J'ai rejoint l'entreprise en tant que plus jeune investisseur jamais embauché. J'y ai grandi. Au fil d'années de débats intenses et de travail partagé, j'ai trouvé des mentors et des amis pour la vie qui m'ont pris sous leur aile et m'ont enseigné ce métier. Ils m'ont appris à viser haut et à prendre de grands risques. Je porterai cela dans ce que je construis : une ambition démesurée, une recherche incessante de la vérité et de la curiosité, et un refus de la complaisance. Travailler aux côtés de fondateurs m'a donné envie de construire quelque chose de moi-même : une entreprise façonnée dès le premier jour autour des convictions que j'ai développées au cours de la dernière décennie. La vie m'a appris à ne pas prendre le temps pour acquis. C'est ainsi que je veux passer le mien. Pourquoi maintenant ? Nous assistons à une nouvelle façon de créer des entreprises à l'ère de l'IA. La recherche et les produits progressent souvent ensemble. Une percée peut ouvrir un marché ou accélérer une entreprise bien plus vite que prévu. Certaines entreprises nécessitent un capital et une puissance de calcul extraordinaires dès le début. D'autres atteignent une échelle significative avec des équipes remarquablement petites. Les règles sur la taille que ces entreprises peuvent atteindre, et à quelle vitesse, sont en train d'être réécrites. Mais au début, la technologie n'est pas prouvée, les ressources requises sont énormes, et la vision semble invraisemblable. C'est ce que j'aime le plus : voir le potentiel dès le début et aider les fondateurs à réaliser toute l'étendue de leur ambition. Plus que jamais, cela commence par une volonté extrême de croire tôt, avec une conviction audacieuse et indépendante dans l'idée technique d'un fondateur avant toute validation de produit ou de marché. Ensuite, cela signifie aider les fondateurs à prendre les plus grands risques, en leur donnant la patience rare et à long terme de mener ces paris à travers l'incertitude, l'ambiguïté et la turbulence, et en servant de tête froide lorsque les enjeux sont les plus élevés. J'ai appris ce type de partenariat chez Sequoia. C'est le fondement de l'entreprise que je construis. Croire avant le consensus Ma fascination pour le potentiel de l'IA a pris racine à Stanford au début et au milieu des années 2010, en étudiant l'informatique et en travaillant dans le laboratoire d'Andrew Ng. Les amitiés que j'ai nouées m'ont connecté à une communauté dont les personnes et les idées contribueraient à façonner l'IA moderne et à construire certaines des entreprises marquantes de notre génération. Ce qui m'est resté, c'est l'écart entre ce que ces personnes voyaient possible et ce que le monde extérieur pouvait imaginer. Je suis attiré par les fondateurs qui poursuivent des ambitions qui semblent impossibles aujourd'hui. Je commence par une question simple : "Et si tout se passe bien ?" Ensuite, nous travaillons ensemble à rebours pour y arriver. En 2023, Deepak et Abhinav ont entrepris de construire un cerveau robotique à usage général chez @SkildAI, avant que l'IA physique ne soit un pari consensuel. Leurs percées du "sim-to-real" m'ont convaincu là où les approches robotiques précédentes avaient échoué. Mais le "volant de données" nécessitait un déploiement à grande échelle. Nous avons rendu la commercialisation aussi urgente que la recherche et avons fait appel à des partenaires stratégiques comme NVIDIA et SoftBank pour soutenir l'ambition. Trois ans plus tard, Skild fait progresser la frontière de l'IA physique avec des revenus annualisés à neuf chiffres. En 2024, Ioannis et Misha ont fondé @reflection_ai avec une idée sur la mise à l'échelle de l'apprentissage par renforcement. Alors que cela se transformait en l'ambition de construire un laboratoire de frontière occidental pour les modèles ouverts, la question difficile était de savoir comment une startup pouvait rivaliser avec des laboratoires dépensant des dizaines de milliards. Une introduction à NVIDIA et de nombreux appels de calcul et événements de recrutement plus tard, l'équipe a construit Beam, désormais l'un des principaux modèles ouverts américains. idees.text_original: I’m starting a new early-stage AI fund, doing what I love: partnering with founders from company formation on bold bets, long before consensus. The fund’s LPs will include Sequoia, Jeff Dean, Sachin Katti, Philip Wong (my Stanford professor and Chief Scientist adviser to TSMC), and others whose work has shaped our industry and how I think about AI’s future. I’ll remain a partner at Sequoia and keep serving on my boards on Sequoia’s behalf. Sequoia has been my home for the past 11 years. I joined as the youngest investor the firm had ever hired. I grew up here. Through years of intense debate and shared work, I found lifelong mentors and friends who took me under their wing and taught me this craft. They taught me to aim high and take big swings. I’ll carry that into what I build: outsized ambition, relentless truth-seeking and curiosity, and a refusal to become complacent. Working alongside founders has made me want to build something of my own: a firm shaped from day one around the convictions I’ve developed over the past decade. Life has taught me not to take time for granted. This is how I want to spend mine. Why now We’re seeing a new way of building companies in today’s AI era. Research and products often advance together. A breakthrough can open a market or accelerate a business far faster than expected. Some companies require extraordinary capital and compute early on. Others reach meaningful scale with remarkably small teams. The rules for how big these businesses can get, and how fast, are being rewritten. But early on, the technology is unproven, the resources required enormous, and the vision seemingly implausible. This is what I love most: seeing the potential right from the beginning, and helping founders realize their full scale of ambition. More than ever, it starts with an extreme willingness to believe early, with bold, independent conviction in a founder’s technical insight before any product or market validation. Then, it means helping founders take the biggest swings, giving the rare, long-term patience to see those bets through uncertainty, ambiguity, and turbulence, and serving as a level head when the stakes are highest. I learned this kind of partnership at Sequoia. It’s the foundation of the firm I’m building. Believing before consensus My fascination with AI’s potential took root at Stanford in the early-to-mid 2010s, studying computer science and working in Andrew Ng’s lab. The friendships I formed connected me to a community whose people and ideas would help shape modern AI and build some of our generation’s defining companies. What stayed with me was the gap between what those people saw was possible and what the wider world could imagine. I’m drawn to founders pursuing ambitions that sound impossible today. I start with a simple question: “What if everything goes right?” Then we work backward together to make it happen. In 2023, Deepak and Abhinav set out to build a general-purpose robot brain at @SkildAI , before physical AI was a consensus bet. Their sim-to-real breakthroughs gave me conviction where earlier robotics approaches had fallen short. But the data flywheel required deployment at scale. We made commercialization as urgent as research and brought in strategic partners like NVIDIA and SoftBank to support the ambition. Three years in, Skild is advancing the frontier of physical AI with nine figures in annualized revenue. In 2024, Ioannis and Misha founded @reflection_ai with an insight into scaling reinforcement learning. As that grew into the ambition to build a Western frontier lab for open models, the hard question was how a startup competes with labs spending tens of billions. An introduction to NVIDIA and many compute calls and recruiting events later, the team has built Beam, now one of the leading US open models. In 2025, Anna et Azalia, the co-creators of AlphaChip, founded @RicursiveAI to design models and hardware together. From day one, we made early customers and ecosystem partners a priority. Today, they are showing order-of-magnitude improvements on real workloads, working with some of the industry’s most consequential players, and reaching a defining inflection point. The ambition keeps growing as these companies scale. @linear has always had a kind of magic to it. Now it’s the system a new generation of AI companies builds on, for teams and agents alike. @tavus saw early that we’d one day talk to AI the way we talk to each other. Today, it’s building the human computing interface for a world of AI colleagues. @Mach_Industries began as hydrogen experiments in an MIT dorm room. It has since become one of the most exciting next-generation defense companies. Making the ambition possible Being a first believer is only the beginning. Compute falls through. A deep-pocketed incumbent makes your mission its top priority. A breakthrough changes the opportunity and the capital required overnight. These are stomach-churning moments, and early belief carries a responsibility to help make the bet work. This is the partnership I love: turning the full ambition into concrete steps. Raising capital, securing compute and strategic partners, recruiting exceptional people, and winning the first customers together. Thinking several moves ahead while solving what’s in front of us. And as breakthroughs open new possibilities, helping founders dream even bigger. Thank you To the founders I’ve worked with: thank you for trusting me and Sequoia to be your first partner and first believer. It’s been the joy of a lifetime, and I can’t wait to keep building together. Thank you to Alfred and Pat for your leadership of Sequoia and your support of my next chapter. So much of what I know, and the investor I’ve become, comes from your guidance and generosity over the years. To Bill, for the close partnership and wealth of knowledge, always wrapped in humility. To Shaun, for showing me how to think deeply and imaginatively. To Michael Moritz, for inspiring 22-year-old me to dream big. To Doug, for teaching me to keep things simple. To Bogie and Jess, for bringing joy to the everyday and perspective on what matters. And to all my Sequoia teammates, for the friendship, camaraderie, and lessons I’ll carry with me. To my family, especially my husband and my brother, who have each started companies of their own: thank you for giving me the courage to take this leap. Let’s get to work!

outils.text_fr: Les travailleurs de six professions accomplissent 79 tâches que la taxonomie professionnelle officielle du gouvernement n'a pas encore ajoutées. Ce travail représente environ 140 milliards de dollars par an en salaires. Cette taxonomie s'appelle O*NET, la base de données du ministère du Travail américain sur les tâches que chaque profession implique. Les travailleurs l'utilisent pour les transitions professionnelles, et les économistes l'utilisent pour estimer quels emplois l'IA va changer. Si les listes sont incomplètes, les estimations le sont aussi. Aujourd'hui, nous publions TaskNet, un catalogue de tâches open-source basé sur O*NET et mis à jour pour refléter l'évolution du travail par l'IA. Construit avec des chercheurs de Stanford, du O*NET Resource Center et du NBER. Merci à @robinsonaisaac @erikbryn @diyi_yang @jennjwang @andreas_h0wpt @Digeconlab @stanfordnlp @stanfordhai @stanfordAIlab pour avoir contribué à ce travail. outils.text_original: Workers in six occupations do 79 tasks the government's official occupational taxonomy has yet to add. That work is worth about $140B a year in wages. Workers use it to help with job transitions, and economists use it to estimate which jobs AI will change. If the lists are incomplete, so are the estimates. Today we're releasing TaskNet, an open-source task catalog built on O*NET and updated for how AI is changing work. Built with researchers from Stanford, the O*NET Resource Center, and NBER.
